The philosopher Jason Brennan has argued persuasively that if it is ethical to donate an organ—an act universally praised—it cannot suddenly become unethical merely because money changes hands. The introduction of compensation does not transform a heroic act into an immoral one. If anything, it extends the pool of heroism to those who might be willing but need material incentive to accept the risk, recovery time, and inconvenience of surgery.

Critics respond that some things should not be "commodified," that placing a price on a kidney degrades human dignity. But this argument proves too much. We pay surgeons to perform transplants, nurses to provide post-operative care, hospitals to maintain sterile operating rooms, and pharmaceutical companies to manufacture immunosuppressants. Every participant in the transplant process is compensated except the one person without whom the entire enterprise is impossible: the organ provider. The current system does not avoid commodification; it merely ensures that the donor is the only party excluded from the economic value their sacrifice creates. This is not dignity. It is exploitation dressed in the language of altruism.

John Stuart Mill articulated the harm principle with clarity: the only legitimate reason for society to restrict individual liberty is to prevent harm to others. A competent adult who, after informed consent, chooses to sell a kidney harms no one. The buyer receives a life-saving organ. The seller receives compensation they value more than the organ they can safely spare. The transaction is positive-sum. Prohibition, by contrast, causes measurable harm: preventable deaths, years of suffering on dialysis, diminished quality of life, and billions of dollars in healthcare costs. The burden of justification falls on those who would override individual choice, and they have not met it.

II. The Shortage Crisis and the Failure of Altruism

The current altruism-based system is failing catastrophically, and no amount of incremental reform has reversed the trend. In the United States, the gap between organ supply and demand has widened in every decade since the passage of NOTA. Campaigns to encourage donation, the introduction of online registries, the adoption of "presumed consent" in some countries, and the expansion of living-donor programs have all helped at the margins, but none has come close to eliminating the shortage.

The numbers are damning. Over 90,000 people await kidney transplants in the United States alone. Median wait times for a kidney exceed five years in many regions and can stretch beyond a decade. During those years of waiting, patients endure dialysis—a grueling, life-shortening, and enormously expensive treatment. Dialysis patients face annual mortality rates of roughly 20 percent. The five-year survival rate on dialysis is approximately 35 percent, compared to over 85 percent for transplant recipients. Each year of delay on the waiting list worsens outcomes even when a transplant eventually occurs, because prolonged dialysis damages the cardiovascular system and other organs irreversibly.

The economic costs are equally staggering. Medicare spends over $50 billion annually on end-stage renal disease, with dialysis consuming the vast majority of those funds. A kidney transplant costs approximately $400,000 in the first year but saves the system money thereafter, because the ongoing cost of immunosuppression and monitoring is a fraction of dialysis expenses. Economists have estimated that each additional kidney transplant saves the healthcare system between $250,000 and $1 million over the patient's lifetime. A market that substantially increased the supply of kidneys would pay for itself many times over, freeing resources for other medical needs.

Nobel laureate economist Gary Becker and Julio Elías estimated in their landmark study that a payment of approximately $15,000 to $30,000 per kidney would be sufficient to eliminate the kidney shortage entirely. Given that the social cost of each patient remaining on dialysis dwarfs this figure, the economic case is overwhelming. The question is not whether society can afford an organ market. The question is whether society can afford to continue without one.

Iran provides the only real-world example of a legal, compensated kidney donation system. Since 1988, Iran has permitted living unrelated donors to receive payment for kidneys, with the government and charitable organizations covering the cost. The result: Iran is the only country in the world that has effectively eliminated its kidney transplant waiting list. While Iran's system has imperfections—many of which stem from insufficient regulation rather than the existence of compensation itself—its core lesson is unmistakable. Financial incentives work. They generate supply. They save lives.

III. Undermining Black Markets and Reducing Exploitation

One of the cruelest ironies of organ prohibition is that it does not prevent organ sales—it merely drives them underground, where the most vulnerable people on earth are subjected to the worst possible conditions. The World Health Organization estimates that roughly 10,000 organs are traded on the black market annually. In these transactions, impoverished sellers in countries like Bangladesh, Pakistan, the Philippines, and parts of Eastern Europe receive a pittance—often $1,000 to $5,000—from brokers who then charge buyers $100,000 or more. Sellers receive no follow-up medical care, no legal protections, and no recourse when complications arise. Buyers face elevated infection risks and uncertain organ quality.

This is the true face of commodification under prohibition—not the hypothetical parade of horrors that opponents of legalization imagine, but an actual, ongoing humanitarian catastrophe. The parallel to other prohibition regimes is instructive. Alcohol prohibition did not eliminate drinking; it empowered organized crime. Drug prohibition has not eliminated drug use; it has fueled violence, incarceration, and unsafe consumption. Organ prohibition has not preserved human dignity; it has created a shadow economy in which dignity is systematically destroyed.

A legal, regulated market would bring organ transactions into the light, subjecting them to the same consumer protections, informed-consent requirements, medical standards, and legal accountability that govern every other medical procedure. Sellers would receive proper screening, surgical care, follow-up treatment, and legal recourse. Prices would be transparent and competitive rather than set by criminal intermediaries. The exploitation that currently characterizes the black market is not an argument against markets per se—it is an argument against black markets, and the most effective way to eliminate a black market is to create a legal alternative.

IV. Addressing the Objection of Coercion and Inequality

The most emotionally compelling objection to organ markets is distributional: critics argue that only the poor would sell and only the rich would buy, creating a system in which poverty effectively coerces individuals into surrendering body parts. This concern deserves serious engagement, but it ultimately fails as an argument for prohibition.

First, the coercion argument proves too much. If financial need renders consent invalid, then we must also prohibit the poor from accepting hazardous employment, enlisting in the military for signing bonuses, or participating in paid clinical trials—all activities that disproportionately attract individuals of lower socioeconomic status and that carry significant physical risk. We do not prohibit these transactions. Instead, we regulate them: we mandate safety standards, ensure informed consent, and provide workers' compensation. The same approach should apply to organ sales.

Second, the concern about inequality in access is real but already present—and worse—under the current system. Wealthy patients can travel abroad for transplant tourism, accessing the very black markets that prohibition creates. They can relocate to regions with shorter waiting lists. They can afford the best dialysis care while they wait, improving their survival odds. Meanwhile, the poor and uninsured die at disproportionate rates on the waiting list. A well-designed market could actually improve equity if structured correctly: the government or insurers could serve as the primary purchasers of organs, distributing them based on medical need rather than ability to pay—exactly as they currently distribute donated organs. The market mechanism would operate on the supply side, incentivizing more people to provide organs, while the allocation side could remain governed by medical criteria.

Third, characterizing compensation as coercion disrespects the agency of the very people it purports to protect. To tell a person living in poverty that they cannot make a decision to improve their financial situation by selling a kidney they can safely spare is not protection—it is paternalism. It presumes that the poor lack the rationality to weigh costs and benefits and that affluent policymakers are better positioned to make decisions about other people's bodies. The philosopher Peter Jaworski captures this point with his "If You Can Give It Away, You Can Sell It" principle: the act of providing a kidney is either acceptable or it is not. If it is acceptable as a gift, the addition of compensation cannot make it unacceptable without invoking a principle that would unravel our entire economic system.

V. Medical Evidence and Safety

Opponents sometimes suggest that living kidney donation is too dangerous to permit financial incentives, as if compensation would cause people to ignore risks they would otherwise weigh carefully. The medical evidence does not support this concern. Living kidney donation is one of the safest surgical procedures in modern medicine. The mortality risk is approximately 0.03 percent—roughly 3 in 10,000—comparable to or lower than many risks people routinely accept for financial compensation. The long-term health outcomes for kidney donors are excellent: large-scale studies, including a landmark Norwegian study tracking donors for over 25 years, have found no significant increase in mortality or end-stage renal disease among donors compared to matched controls.

Moreover, a legal market would almost certainly improve safety, not diminish it. Currently, desperate patients resort to poorly screened organs obtained through black-market channels with minimal medical oversight. Legal markets would involve rigorous donor screening, sophisticated tissue matching, proper surgical facilities, mandatory follow-up care, and transparent outcome tracking. The same regulatory infrastructure that ensures the safety of blood and plasma sales—which compensate providers and function without scandal—could be adapted for organ transactions.

VI. Designing a Just Market

Advocating for an organ market does not mean advocating for an unregulated free-for-all. The most persuasive proposals envision a carefully structured system with robust safeguards:

Informed consent protocols would require comprehensive education about risks, recovery time, and long-term health implications, with mandatory waiting periods and psychological evaluation.

A single-payer purchasing model could be implemented, in which the government or designated insurers purchase organs at a fixed price and allocate them based on medical criteria, separating the supply-side incentive from the allocation decision.

Vendor protections would include guaranteed health insurance for donation-related complications, disability coverage, and legal recourse for malpractice.

Eligibility standards would restrict sales to competent adults meeting medical fitness criteria, with prohibitions on sales by minors, the cognitively impaired, or the medically unsuitable.

Price regulation could set compensation at levels sufficient to incentivize supply without creating irresistible financial pressure—perhaps a combination of direct payment, tax credits, tuition assistance, or contributions to retirement accounts.

Such a system is not utopian. It is modeled on existing regulatory frameworks for compensated medical transactions that already function safely and effectively.

VII. The Moral Weight of Preventable Death

Ultimately, the case for organ markets must be weighed against the alternative—and the alternative is the status quo, which kills people. This is not a theoretical harm. It is a body count. Over 7,000 Americans die annually waiting for organ transplants. Globally, the figure is many times larger. Each of these deaths represents not an act of God or an unavoidable tragedy but a policy choice: the choice to maintain a prohibition that suppresses supply in deference to moral intuitions that do not survive scrutiny.

The philosopher James Stacey Taylor has argued that those who oppose organ markets bear a profound moral burden: they must explain why their discomfort with commercialization outweighs the lives that could be saved. They must justify, to each person who dies on a waiting list, why the abstract principle of non-commodification mattered more than their survival. This is an explanation that, in my view, cannot be satisfactorily given.

Conclusion

The prohibition on organ sales is a relic of moral intuitions that, however well-intentioned, have produced catastrophic results. It violates individual autonomy by preventing competent adults from making decisions about their own bodies. It perpetuates a shortage that kills thousands of people every year. It drives desperate patients and impoverished sellers into black markets characterized by exploitation, medical negligence, and criminal violence. It costs healthcare systems billions of dollars annually in avoidable dialysis expenses. And it does all of this in the name of a "dignity" that is nowhere to be found in the suffering of patients dying on waiting lists or in the squalid back-room surgeries of underground organ trafficking.

A regulated market in human organs would not solve every problem in transplant medicine. But it would save thousands of lives per year, respect the bodily autonomy of donors and recipients alike, channel transactions into safe and transparent medical settings, and allocate a scarce, life-saving resource with far greater efficiency and equity than the current system achieves. The moral case for legalization is not merely strong. In the face of so much preventable death and suffering, it is overwhelming. The question we should be asking is not whether we can afford to try a market in organs. The question is how we justify, morally and practically, refusing to do so for one more day.

The Moral Case for a Free Market in Human Organs

A Speech

Ladies and gentlemen,

Every ten minutes, another name is added to the national organ transplant waiting list. Every day, seventeen people on that list die. Not because medicine has failed them. Not because no willing donor exists. They die because we made it illegal to save them.

Let that sink in.

We have constructed a legal regime — born from good intentions, I grant you — that criminalizes the voluntary exchange between a willing seller and a desperate buyer, and we call this ethics. I am here today to argue that it is anything but. I am here to make the case — the moral case, the economic case, the humanitarian case — for a fully legal, regulated, free market in human organs for transplantation.

I. The Crisis We Have Created

In the United States alone, over 100,000 people languish on organ waiting lists. The median wait for a kidney — the most needed organ — can exceed five years. In many regions, it is longer. During that wait, patients endure grueling dialysis sessions, three or four times a week, watching their bodies deteriorate, their careers collapse, their families strain under the weight of chronic illness.

And here is the bitter irony: kidneys are not scarce. Every healthy human being has two. Millions of people around the world would willingly part with one — if they were permitted to be compensated for their sacrifice, their pain, their risk, and their recovery time.

But we don't permit it. The National Organ Transplant Act of 1984 made it a federal crime to exchange organs for "valuable consideration." Similar laws exist in virtually every developed nation. We rely instead on altruistic donation — and altruistic donation, for all its nobility, has never come close to meeting demand. Not in 1984. Not today. Not ever.

The waiting list does not shrink. It grows. Year after year after year. The dead accumulate. And we pat ourselves on the back for maintaining the moral high ground.

I ask you: what moral high ground is built on graves?

II. The Principle of Bodily Autonomy

Let me start with the most fundamental argument — the argument from self-ownership.

We hold, in virtually every other domain of life, that competent adults have sovereignty over their own bodies. A woman may choose to carry a pregnancy or not. A person may donate blood, plasma, sperm, or eggs — and be compensated for all of these. A young man or woman may enlist in the armed forces, accepting the risk of death and dismemberment, for a salary. A person may work in a coal mine, on an oil rig, or as a test subject in a pharmaceutical trial — all activities that carry real risk of bodily harm — in exchange for money.

We allow people to give a kidney away for free. We celebrate them when they do. We call them heroes.

But the moment they ask for compensation — the moment a single mother considers alleviating her poverty by selling a kidney she can medically spare — we call it exploitation, we call it commodification, and we send in the prosecutors.

Explain this to me. If it is noble to surrender a kidney for nothing, how does it become ignoble to surrender a kidney for something? The organ is the same. The surgery is the same. The recipient's life is saved just the same.

What changes is only that the donor is also made better off.

The prohibition on organ sales does not protect bodily autonomy. It violates it. It tells competent adults: you may take this risk for free, but you may not take this same risk for compensation. That is not autonomy. That is paternalism of the most lethal kind.

III. The Economic Argument — Supply, Demand, and the Price of Prohibition

Economics teaches a lesson so basic it should not need repeating, yet apparently it does: when you set the legal price of a valuable commodity at zero, you get a shortage.

That is precisely what we have done with organs. We have imposed a price ceiling of zero on one of the most valuable and life-saving goods in existence, and we are shocked — shocked — that supply does not meet demand.

A legal market would change this overnight. Not metaphorically. Literally. Studies by economists such as Nobel laureate Gary Becker and Julio Elías have estimated that a payment of roughly $15,000 to $30,000 for a living kidney donation would be sufficient to eliminate the kidney shortage entirely in the United States. That figure — let us put it in perspective — is a fraction of the cost of years of dialysis, which runs to hundreds of thousands of dollars per patient and is largely borne by Medicare, which is to say, by all of us.

A market in organs would not merely save lives. It would save money. It would liberate patients from dialysis. It would return them to productive life, to their families, to their work. It would relieve the enormous fiscal burden on public health systems.

The economists are not divided on this. The question is not whether a market would increase supply. The question is only whether we have the courage to allow it.

IV. Confronting the Objections

Now, I know the objections. I have heard them all, and I take them seriously. Let me address them head on.

"A market would exploit the poor."

This is the objection raised most frequently, and it is the one that most deserves scrutiny — because it is, at bottom, an argument that we should protect poor people by taking away their choices.

Consider what we are really saying: a poor person who wishes to sell a kidney for $30,000 — a sum that could pay off debts, fund an education, start a business, secure housing — should be prevented from doing so for their own good. Meanwhile, that same person is free to work backbreaking manual labor, enlist in the military, or participate in dangerous clinical trials.

We do not ban these activities to protect the poor. We regulate them. We insist on informed consent, safety standards, and fair dealing.

Why should organ sales be any different?

Furthermore, let us ask: who suffers most under the current system? It is the poor. It is the unconnected. It is those who lack access to the informal networks and social capital that facilitate living donation among the affluent. Wealthy patients travel abroad for transplant tourism in unregulated black markets. Poor patients stay on dialysis and die.

The current system doesn't protect the poor from exploitation. It condemns them to the worst outcomes on both sides of the transaction — as potential donors who cannot be compensated, and as patients who cannot access transplants.

"It commodifies the human body."

We already commodify the human body. We pay surgeons handsomely for their skilled hands. We pay nurses for their labor. We pay pharmaceutical companies for the drugs that keep transplanted organs from being rejected. We pay hospitals for the operating rooms. Everyone in the transplant chain is compensated — except the one person without whom the entire enterprise is impossible: the donor.

We have not prevented commodification. We have merely insisted that the donor — the person who makes the greatest sacrifice — must be the only participant who receives nothing. That is not high-minded ethics. That is an injustice.

"It would corrupt the existing altruistic system."

This is an empirical claim, and the evidence does not clearly support it. Iran — the one country in the world that permits compensated kidney donation — has effectively eliminated its kidney waiting list. Meanwhile, altruistic donation in Iran continues. Compensation and altruism are not mutually exclusive. They are complementary. A rising tide of organs lifts all patients.

V. What a Legal Market Would Look Like

I am not advocating for an unregulated bazaar. I am advocating for what we build in every other domain where the stakes are high: a regulated market with robust safeguards.

Here is what such a system might include:

  • Mandatory informed consent — thorough medical and psychological evaluation of every potential seller, with waiting periods and independent counsel.
  • Centralized oversight — a regulated exchange, perhaps administered or supervised by a body like UNOS, to ensure transparency and fairness.
  • Health protections for sellers — guaranteed lifelong health insurance for any complications arising from donation, funded by the system.
  • Price floors, not ceilings — ensuring that compensation is meaningful and fair, not exploitative.
  • Anti-coercion provisions — strict penalties for any form of pressure, fraud, or duress.
  • Equitable distribution — organs allocated to recipients based on medical need, not ability to pay, with government or insurance covering the cost of procurement just as they currently cover the cost of transplant surgery.

This is not radical. This is how we handle every other complex market involving risk and human welfare. We regulate. We protect. And we allow the transaction that saves lives.

VI. The Moral Reckoning

Let me close with this.

There is a concept in moral philosophy called the doctrine of the double effect — the idea that we may tolerate certain costs if the intended outcome is sufficiently good and the alternative is sufficiently terrible.

But our current prohibition does not even rise to that standard. The costs of prohibition are catastrophic: thousands of preventable deaths per year, immeasurable suffering, billions in healthcare expenditures. And the benefits? A feeling of moral purity. The comfort of knowing that we have not "commercialized" the human body — even as patients commercialize their suffering in crowdfunding campaigns, even as black markets flourish in the shadows, even as bodies pile up on waiting lists.

We are not choosing between a perfect world and a market in organs. We are choosing between a black market in organs — which already exists, which is exploitative, which is dangerous, which is corrupt — and a legal market in organs, which we can regulate, oversee, and make safe and fair.

Every year we delay, six thousand Americans die who did not have to. Each one of them had a name. Each one of them had a family. Each one of them might have been saved if we had the moral courage to question a taboo.

The philosopher Peter Singer has said that if we can prevent something bad from happening without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it. We can prevent thousands of deaths a year. The cost is only our squeamishness.

It is time to legalize the market in human organs.

It is time to stop sentencing the sick to death in the name of a moral purity that does not save a single life.

It is time to trust free people to make free choices about their own bodies — and to let those choices save the lives of others.

The waiting list is a death sentence written in law. We have the power to commute it. Let us find the courage to do so.

Thank you.

The Case for Legalizing a Free Market in Human Organs: Empowering Autonomy, Ending Shortages, and Saving Lives

In the United States alone, over 100,000 individuals languish on waiting lists for life-saving organ transplants, with nearly 20 dying each day while waiting. The time has come to reject this prohibitionist mindset and fully legalize a free market in human organs for transplantation. Such a policy would maximize individual autonomy by affirming people's rights over their own bodies, drastically alleviate chronic shortages by incentivizing supply, and improve health outcomes through faster access and better-quality organs. At the heart of the argument for an organ market is the principle of bodily autonomy—the fundamental right of individuals to make decisions about their own bodies without coercive interference from the state. Currently, laws like the National Organ Transplant Act of 1984 criminalize the buying and selling of organs, forcing reliance on voluntary altruism. This paternalistic approach undermines personal liberty, akin to banning consensual adult contracts in other realms. Just as individuals are free to sell their hair, plasma, or even risk their lives in hazardous professions like deep-sea welding for compensation, they should have the sovereign right to sell renewable or non-vital organs, such as kidneys or portions of the liver, provided they are of sound mind and fully informed. Autonomy is not absolute in a vacuum; it thrives in a framework of consent and regulation. A legal market would require rigorous medical evaluations, psychological screenings, and contracts to prevent coercion, ensuring that sellers exercise true agency rather than desperation. Beyond autonomy, a free market in organs would decisively address the dire shortages plaguing transplant systems worldwide. The altruistic model has failed spectacularly: despite public campaigns and opt-out donor registries in some countries, supply remains woefully inadequate. In 2022, for instance, only about 40,000 transplants occurred globally, while millions suffer from end-stage organ failure. Economic theory explains this shortfall—altruism alone cannot scale to meet demand in a resource-scarce environment. Introducing market incentives would transform potential donors into willing suppliers. Historical precedents abound: paid blood plasma donation in the U.S. sustains a robust supply without compromising safety, and Iran's regulated kidney market since 1988 has virtually eliminated waiting lists for that organ. In a free market, compensation—whether cash, tax credits, or insurance premiums—would motivate healthy individuals to donate, particularly those in financial need who might otherwise hesitate. Critics decry this as exploiting the poor, but prohibition already drives a black market where organs fetch exorbitant prices from desperate brokers, preying on the vulnerable without oversight. Legalization would democratize access, regulate prices to prevent gouging, and channel supply through ethical channels, ultimately flooding the system with organs and slashing wait times from years to months.

Finally, an organ market would yield superior health outcomes by accelerating transplants and enhancing organ quality. Prolonged waiting exacerbates patient deterioration; for kidneys, the average wait exceeds three years, during which dialysis takes a heavy toll, reducing post-transplant survival rates. A market-driven system would prioritize efficiency: donors could be matched swiftly with recipients via competitive bidding or centralized exchanges, minimizing cold ischemia time—the period organs spend outside the body, which directly impacts viability. Moreover, financial incentives would encourage healthier donors to participate, as sellers seek premium compensation for well-maintained organs, leading to fewer rejections and complications. Empirical evidence from Iran's model supports this: transplant success rates there match or exceed those in altruistic systems, with lower infection risks due to traceable supply chains. In contrast, the black market's unregulated organs often come from coerced or unhealthy sources, heightening dangers. A legal framework could incorporate safeguards like minimum compensation floors to protect sellers and quality certifications to benefit buyers, turning a humanitarian crisis into a model of medical innovation. The result? Fewer deaths, reduced healthcare costs from prolonged treatments, and a more equitable allocation where urgency and compatibility, not lottery, determine access.

Opponents may invoke slippery slopes—fearing coerced sales or a dystopia of organ farms—but these specters dissolve under scrutiny. Exploitation is already rampant in the shadows of prohibition; legalization brings it into the light, where labor laws, anti-trafficking measures, and ethical oversight can intervene. Just as markets for surrogacy or gametes have been regulated without descending into chaos, an organ market can be structured with caps on sales, bans on vital organs like hearts (while alive), and subsidies for low-income recipients to ensure fairness. The moral hazard of "selling body parts" pales against the ethical imperative to end needless suffering; after all, we already commodify bodies through military service, athletics, and even cosmetic surgery industries.

In conclusion, fully legalizing a free market in human organs is not a radical departure but a rational evolution, one that honors autonomy, obliterates shortages, and elevates outcomes for the greater good. By empowering individuals to trade what is rightfully theirs, we would rescue tens of thousands from the brink of death and redefine transplantation as a triumph of human ingenuity. Policymakers must act now: pilot programs, international collaborations, and legislative reform are essential to implement this life-affirming system. Title: The Moral and Practical Imperative of Legalizing a Free Market in Human Organs

Introduction
Every day, thousands of individuals worldwide suffer and die due to a severe shortage of transplantable organs. The current altruistic donation system, relying on voluntary donations and deceased registries, is failing to meet demand, resulting in prolonged waiting lists, preventable deaths, and thriving black markets. To address this crisis, society must reconsider its moral and legal stance on organ sales. Legalizing a free market in human organs would maximize individual autonomy, alleviate shortages, and improve health outcomes. By embracing a regulated free market, we can save lives while respecting personal freedom and ensuring equity.

Maximizing Autonomy: The Right to Choose
The principle of bodily autonomy lies at the core of individual freedom. Just as people have the right to engage in consensual activities, donate blood, or sell gametes, they should be permitted to sell organs. Critics argue that commodifying the body undermines human dignity, but autonomy requires that individuals, free from coercion, may make decisions about their own flesh. Permitting financial incentives for organ donation does not automatically lead to exploitation; rather, it empowers those in need of income—especially the economically disadvantaged—to make informed, voluntary choices. As philosopher Peter Singer has argued, denying individuals the right to sell organs merely to protect them from hypothetical exploitation is paternalistic. Informed consent, rigorous disclosure of risks, and counseling safeguards can ensure that donors act autonomously, turning their bodily capital into a means of improving their own lives.

Alleviating Shortages Through Incentives
The altruistic system’s failure is stark: in the U.S. alone, over 100,000 people await transplants, with 17 dying daily due to shortage. A free market would bridge this gap by incentivizing supply. Financial compensation—a proven motivator in blood and plasma donation—would attract more living donors and encourage families of deceased individuals to donate. For instance, Iran’s system of compensated kidney donation has eliminated its waiting list, demonstrating the viability of such models. Critics warn that markets might exploit the poor, but this overlooks the agency of individuals. Offering compensation is not coercion; it is recognizing the sacrifice of donation. Moreover, a legal market would operate transparently, with standardized compensation and protections against undue influence, ensuring equitable participation by all socioeconomic groups.

Improving Outcomes Through Regulation
Legitimizing the organ market would simultaneously enhance safety and outcomes. Currently, desperation drives many to illicit black markets, where organs are harvested under unsanitary conditions, leading to infections, deaths, and exploitation. A regulated system would require medical oversight, ensuring donors receive proper care and recipients obtain healthy organs. Centralized registries and standardized protocols would streamline matching, reduce waiting times, and improve transplant success rates. Additionally, transparency would foster public trust, encouraging more participate. For example, regulated markets for blood and tissue have proven safe and effective, suggesting that similar frameworks could be adapted for solid organs. By eliminating black markets, a legal system would protect vulnerable populations while maximizing the utility of organs.

Addressing Counterarguments
Opponents raise valid concerns: exploitation of the poor, commodification of the body, and inequity. However, these issues can be mitigated through thoughtful regulation. Safeguards such as mandatory counseling, age restrictions, and minimum compensation standards would protect donors. Furthermore, a non-profit intermediary could manage transactions to prevent price gouging and ensure fairness. The moral imperative to save lives must outweigh abstract objections to commodification. Allowing the market to function does not reduce humans to commodities but rather respects their agency in choosing how to use their bodies. As with other difficult choices—such as service in the military or high-risk labor—society can honor autonomy while providing safety nets.

Conclusion
The current organ shortage represents a humanitarian crisis that demands bold solutions. Legalizing a free market in human organs would harness the power of individual choice and economic incentives to save lives. By maximizing autonomy, addressing shortages, and improving outcomes through regulation, such a system aligns with both ethical imperatives and practical realities. To uphold human dignity, we must trust individuals to make decisions about their own bodies and ensure that those choices contribute to the greater good. The time has come to embrace a regulated organ market—not as a last resort, but as a moral priority.
